overview: This file concerns the possible U.S. recognition of Japan’s postwar meat-inspection system and the conditions under which Japanese meat and meat-food products could become eligible for importation into the United States. A Department of Agriculture covering memorandum forwards to the Department of State a copy of its response to Lieutenant Colonel Marion W. Scothorn of the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers in Tokyo. The response explains that recognition required Japanese laws, implementing regulations, English translations, and a Foreign Service report demonstrating substantial equivalence with the U.S. system; it also discusses product restrictions, official export certificates, and relevant regulations and instructional materials.

subfiles.title: Memorandum forwarding information on Japanese meat inspection
subfiles.from: H. H. Pas, Acting Chief, Special Projects Section, Meat Inspection Division, Bureau of Animal Industry
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State, Division of Protective Services
subfiles.about: Forwards the Agriculture Department’s reply to Lieutenant Colonel Marion W. Scothorn concerning U.S. recognition of Japan’s meat-inspection system.
subfiles.summary: Pas reports that Lieutenant Colonel Scothorn, stationed in Tokyo, has asked about the current U.S. position on recognition of the Japanese meat-inspection system. Copies of the Bureau of Animal Industry’s reply are enclosed for the Department of State’s information. The memorandum was routed through the Office of Foreign Agricultural Relations and received by the Division of Protective Services on December 16, 1949.

subfiles.title: Letter to Scothorn on recognition of Japan’s meat-inspection system
subfiles.from: H. H. Pas, Acting Chief, Special Projects Section, Meat Inspection Division, Bureau of Animal Industry
subfiles.to: Lieutenant Colonel Marion W. Scothorn, Chief, Veterinary Affairs Division, General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Explains the evidence and procedures required for U.S. recognition of Japan’s meat-inspection system and subsequent importation of Japanese meat products.
subfiles.summary: Responding to Scothorn’s letter of November 25, Pas states that the bureau lacks enough information to answer his numbered questions directly. He explains that a foreign government must submit its enabling law, regulations, translations, and evidence of effective administration through diplomatic channels so that the United States can determine whether its inspection system is substantially equivalent to the American system. A Foreign Service officer would prepare the in-country report, probably relying on Scothorn’s technical assistance. Even after recognition, Japanese products would have to comply with BAI Order 373 and carry an approved official inspection certificate; the letter also forwards U.S. regulations, sample foreign certificates, and information about Agriculture Department films.

interest: The file offers a concise view of how U.S. sanitary regulation, diplomacy, and occupation administration intersected in postwar Japan. It is especially useful for showing that recognition depended not merely on the existence of Japanese legislation but also on evidence that the system operated effectively and was substantially equivalent to U.S. inspection. The anticipated reliance on a SCAP veterinary officer for technical information illustrates the practical role of occupation personnel in reconnecting Japan with international trade, while the discussion of certificates and product-specific restrictions documents the administrative mechanics of possible meat exports to the United States.
